Existing reviews have emphasized either emerging membrane ma - terials without systematically discussing the commercially available ones or focused primarily on high-pressure separations (nanofiltration and reverse osmosis [21] ) without integrating modified micro- and ul - trafiltration or downstream concentrate handling. The presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in surface water has been widely reported in recent years. Many techniques, e.g., adsorption, have been investigated to remove PFAS from contaminated waters. However, the underlying impacts of PFAS on conventional drinking water treatment have been overlooked so far. In this study, we hypothesized whether PFAS have significant impacts on algae in surface water, which in turn may influence the performance of typical treatment processes (e.g., coagulation/membrane filtration). There - fore, we sampled a representative surface water (drinking water source) in Beijing, China, and dosed 2 repre - sentative PFAS compounds, at environment concentrations, to conduct bench-scale treatment tests. Results showed that the presence of PFAS caused larger flocs during coagulation and more severe ultrafiltration (UF) membrane fouling, compared with a control solution without PFAS. Specifically, PFAS at a low concentration (0.1 μ g/L) led to the greatest influence on floc growth and UF membrane fouling; compared with the solution without PFAS, the floc size increased by 1.6 times and membrane flux declined more than 10%. These effects were evidenced by the stress response of algae under PFAS stimulus, secreting more biopolymers (mainly polysaccharides), rather than by PFAS directly.

However, fundamental studies under the in ﬂuence of variable NOM characteristics and inorganic anions have often been overlooked. This is important given NOM characteristics (such as charge density and molecular weight) and inorganic anions concentrations are geographically and seasonally variable.
